editorial.headline: Underwriting, Corporate Action, and the Bali PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers securities underwriting and corporate-action advice, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Securities underwriting is not simply a transaction at the moment securities are offered to the public. It is an activity spanning the preparation and support of an offering, alongside work connected to the corporate actions of companies preparing for, or already having made, a public offering. In practical terms, its scope includes underwriting securities issues and advising on their issuance, as well as on mergers, consolidations, acquisitions, and restructurings. It also encompasses other activities determined and/or approved by the Financial Services Authority.

The registration follows the activity itself: the party carrying out securities underwriting and the related corporate-action work. Its scope is therefore defined by a close relationship with companies at a public-offering stage, rather than by a single isolated service. The code is open across the full stated business-scale range—Micro, Small, Medium, and Large—so the formal scale classification does not narrow the underlying description of the work. What matters is that the registered business is undertaking the underwriting or the connected advisory and corporate-action activity described here.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is full foreign ownership, not a partial allowance framed as openness. The relevant national source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the activity at national level, the essential point is that the code does not impose a lower foreign-equity ceiling in the record.

Bali’s position is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Large scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High/High, which is why the Bali assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than a prohibition. A foreign-owned business registering this activity in Bali is therefore not stopped by the stated Bali moratorium; the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ownership figure in the record.
